content.text: A re-render is React calling your component again to work out what the UI should look like. The DOM changes only in the commit phase, and only where the new output differs from the previous one. What really throws DOM nodes away is a change of component type or key at the same spot in the tree, not the re-render itself.

A bug report lands on Monday morning: "The search box loses focus after every letter." The team's first theory sounds reasonable: the page re-renders on every keystroke, so React must be rebuilding the input each time. Someone wraps half the page in
, the render count drops, and the bug stays exactly where it was. The real cause had nothing to do with how often the page rendered, and seeing why takes the model React actually runs on.
The belief goes like this: every time a component re-renders, React rebuilds its part of the DOM, so every re-render is expensive, and a React developer's main job is to prevent them.
It's an easy belief to pick up. In the jQuery days, re-rendering a widget often meant replacing its

, which really did throw the old nodes away. React DevTools adds to it: turn on update highlighting and every component that rendered flashes, which looks a lot like repainting. And the myth is half true: rendering does cost something, and in a few specific cases React really does recreate DOM nodes. The mistake is treating those cases as the default.
React's docs split every screen update into three steps: something triggers a render, React renders your components, and React commits the result to the DOM. Only the last step touches the page.

The docs name two triggers: the initial render, and a state update in the component or in one of its ancestors. A parent re-rendering is enough; the child's props don't have to change. Context changes cause renders too, and the next article in this path covers every trigger.
Step 2: the render phase calls your functions

is React calling your components: the one whose state changed, then every component it returns, recursively. The result is a fresh description of the UI made of plain JavaScript objects, not DOM nodes. React compares it with the previous one, position by position, to find what is different; this comparison is usually called
. Nothing on screen has changed yet.
Step 3: the commit phase applies only the difference

, React applies the minimal set of DOM operations that makes the page match the new output. On the first render, that means inserting every node. On a re-render, a node that didn't change is left alone, with its typed text and focus. If the output is identical, the commit doesn't touch the DOM at all. Then the browser paints, which React's docs deliberately call painting, not rendering, to avoid this exact confusion.

blocks.title: See renders and DOM writes side by side

content.text: Turn on "Highlight updates when components render" in React DevTools and open the Elements panel of Chrome DevTools. React DevTools outlines every component that rendered; the Elements panel flashes only the DOM nodes that changed. Seeing how small the second set is makes the model stick.

Where the real cost of a re-render is

A re-render does cost something: React runs your component and everything below it, then compares the results. For most components that's a few function calls and small objects. It gets noticeable when render does heavy work, like filtering thousands of rows on every keystroke, or when a component near the top re-renders a large subtree very often. React's docs offer opt-in tools like
for that, and also say not to optimize prematurely: if a re-render causes no perceptible lag,
, React calls your components twice in development to surface impure code, so the
log above appears twice per click. Production builds skip this, so never judge performance by a development build.
How to apply it in your project
A component rendering again after a state change is React doing its job. It's a problem only when you can see or measure it: typing lags, a list stutters, or the Profiler shows a slow interaction.
Record the slow interaction with the Profiler tab of React DevTools. It shows which components rendered and how long each one took, so you fix the slow one instead of wrapping everything.

items.text: A re-render is React calling your component again to compute the UI; on its own, it changes nothing on screen.
The commit phase writes only the differences to the DOM, so unchanged nodes keep their identity, focus and text.
